description: We’re Project Burhan, five students who share a curiosity about the night sky. Our degrees span computer engineering and computer science, data science, mathematics and AI policy. That mix shaped the project: engineering for the data pipeline, mathematics for the measurements, and a policy mindset for honesty about what the tool can prove. Some of us study variable stars and are building a telescope. “Burhan” means proof in Arabic, and proof is what we set out to build for every stargazer.
summary:
SPHEREx records a different wavelength at every spot, so blinking raw frames shows color, not motion. The tool compares like with like (visit stacks, wavelength filter, difference views) and overlays Gaia, SIMBAD, VSX and JPL asteroid predictions. Type any object name or sky position and the server builds that field on request.

It is a measurement, not just a viewer. We measure each object's position in every image, with error bars set by isolated reference stars, and test it against where catalogs predict it should be. All four targets with measurable motion match catalog motions within 2 sigma, including Epsilon Indi B, whose roughly 1-pixel shift our early estimate called undetectable, and WISE 0855, too faint for single images, which we measure by fitting SPHEREx's star-image model across each visit. RW Aurigae is correctly called a brightness change; saturated R Draconis is reported as unmeasurable, not "no motion."

We test on stars the tool was never tuned on: 65 of 73 Gaia field stars move as predicted, including all 14 uncrowded ones. The 8 failures have close neighbors blending their light. We report them, plus error bars running about 1.4 times too small. Every result is for a known object; we claim no discoveries.
details:
What it does. Our tool lets anyone look at SPHEREx images of a patch of sky over time and see whether anything in it moves or changes. The challenge is that SPHEREx never takes the same picture twice: each image samples a different wavelength at each point on the detector, so blinking consecutive frames shows color, not motion. We compare like with like. All images from one roughly six-month visit are averaged into a clean, north-up picture. Users can play the visits like a flipbook, blink any two, or subtract one from another, and a wavelength filter blinks only images taken at the same wavelength across visits. Every single exposure can also be opened, with its time, detector, wavelength and quality-flag overlay. Any view can be shared as a link.

How it works. For each field we gather every public SPHEREx image, cut out the field, subtract the zodiacal light model and leftover background, and blank flagged pixels. Saturated pixels are kept, because the SPHEREx Explanatory Supplement says their values come from readouts taken before saturation, so they are usable but less precise. We measure each object in every single image, in that image's own pixels, because resampling blurs positions, and fit nearby catalog stars at the same time so they cannot pull the result. Error bars include the scatter of isolated Gaia reference stars and a shared per-visit error. For WISE 0855, too faint for single images, we fit SPHEREx's own PSF model to all of a visit's images at once. A motion fit and a wavelength-aware brightness test then give one of six verdicts, each with an explicit rule.

Checking itself against catalogs. Each object's measured position is shown next to where Gaia (or, for WISE 0855, Kirkpatrick et al. 2021) predicts it on that date. All four measurable challenge targets agree with their catalogs: Epsilon Indi B (0.9 and 0.6 sigma), WISE 0855 (0.2 and 0.6 sigma; a motion detection of about 7 sigma from three visits) and Barnard's Star (2.3 sigma in RA, our weakest) show the expected motion, and RW Aurigae shows none, as catalogued. Epsilon Indi B moves only about 1.1 pixels in 1.4 years. RW Aurigae is called a brightness change, not motion. Saturated R Draconis is reported as unmeasurable instead of "no motion."

Measuring its own accuracy. We measured every Gaia star down to G = 17 in each field and scored it as we score the targets. All 100 were recovered in the four scored fields. Of the 73 stars not used to set the error bars, 65 move as Gaia predicts, and all 14 stars with no close neighbor pass. The 8 that fail are all crowded (7 in Barnard's Star's field, 1 in WISE 0855's), and we list them. Our error bars are slightly too small overall (real scatter is about 1.4 times the error bar), and the scoreboard says so.

Catalog layers. Gaia, SIMBAD and AAVSO VSX markers, plus known asteroids predicted by JPL's Small-Body Identification service, appear on the images, and a panel explains each object. Asteroid markers are predictions, not detections, and most are very faint (V mostly above 21).

Tools. Python (Astropy, astroquery, photutils, reproject, NumPy, SciPy, FastAPI) and a static website in HTML, JavaScript and CSS. Data: SPHEREx (NASA/IPAC IRSA), Gaia DR3, SIMBAD, AAVSO VSX, CatWISE2020, JPL, Kirkpatrick et al. 2021.

Creativity and care. The wavelength problem is built into the core, not added on. We also corrected ourselves: a test with more images showed our error bars were too small, and we changed the fit. SIMBAD swaps the Gaia IDs of RW Aurigae A and B; we verified the right assignment against ALMA positions (Rodriguez et al. 2018).

Limits. Pixels are 6.15 arcseconds, so close binaries blur together. Crowded stars have a constant position offset, and 8 fail the motion test, probably because we fit neighbors with a round Gaussian while SPHEREx's real PSF is asymmetric. Saturated targets give poor brightness. Only 51-pixel fields are built for the five targets. A server that builds any typed position works in local tests but is not public, and flagging objects in no catalog is not built. We found no new objects; the tool reproduces known motions and measures how far to trust them.

Impact. Backyard Worlds volunteers found most known brown dwarfs by blinking images. This makes SPHEREx data blinkable by anyone, with measurements to check what they see.
